---
title: Data modules
description: "Supply named train, validate, test, and predict sources from Parquet, Arrow, Polars, or DuckDB."
---

A data module groups sources into named splits: training learns the model,
validation selects it, testing evaluates it, and prediction scores new records.
RelFlow uses Lightning, a training framework, to iterate these sources in batches.
Passing a module to a model loop binds it to that model's schema and batch size.
Each row is one observation prepared as in
[Prepare observations](../learn/prepare-observations.qmd): nested lists and
structs stay inside the row, the application assembles each history and
chooses the splits, and training files carry settled labels while prediction
files omit them. The data module does not join transaction tables into a
history.

The examples continue the
[transaction model](../learn/add-transaction-history.qmd). Its `payment_id`
column remains a source column without becoming a model field.

## Arrow

Pass Parquet file paths to `ArrowDataModule`:

```python
import relflow as rf

# Reuse the history model; each file row has the nested structure above.
data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    train="payments/history/train.parquet",
    validate="payments/history/validation.parquet",
)
```

Nested structs and lists remain part of each observation. Existing in-memory
`pyarrow.Table` objects are also supported.

## Bind a model when the loop starts

Configure the sources independently of the model, then pass the data module
to the model's loop:

```python
data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    train="payments/history/train.parquet",
    validate="payments/history/validation.parquet",
)
model.fit(data, batch_size=128, max_epochs=30)
```

`fit`, `validate`, `test`, and data-module `predict` bind an unbound module
before setup and loading. `PolarsDataModule`, `DuckDBDataModule`,
`CustomDataModule`, and `SyntheticDataModule` support the same lifecycle.
The loop's model owns the schema and batch size used to prepare batches.

For direct loader access outside a loop, call `data.bind(model)` first.
Reading the model-dependent schema or batch size, or creating a configured
loader while unbound, raises `RuntimeError`.
Calling `bind` again with the same model is harmless; binding to a different
model raises `ValueError`. Create a separate data module for each model in a
comparison, including a separately loaded copy of the same artifact.

Native Lightning `Trainer` loops also bind in data-module `setup` using the
attached RelFlow model. Their optimizer requirements remain those described
in [Training options](training-options.qmd#configure-optimization-and-callbacks).

The default shuffle window is resolved once at binding as
`max(model.batch_size * 32, 4096)` rows. For an unbound module, a loop's
explicit batch size is applied before binding. An explicit `shuffle_rows`
value takes precedence. Changing batch size after binding changes subsequent
loader batches but does not resize that window; set `shuffle_rows` explicitly
when comparing shuffle behavior across runs. This window applies to streaming
sources; in-memory Arrow tables use a full permutation. Streaming shuffle can
buffer up to twice the window, so account for that memory when sizing it.

## Splits and preparation

Supply `train`, `validate`, `test`, and `predict` independently; at least one is
required. Each supplied path or source belongs to its named split. Training
shuffles by default. The other splits do not. Set model
batch size on the loop, for example `model.fit(data, batch_size=128, max_epochs=30)`.
Arrow data modules read the model's current size whenever they create loaders;
see [Batch size](training-options.qmd#batch-size) for overrides on the other loops.

Choose splits before constructing the module. For time-based evaluation, define
an observation cutoff, build features only from information available then, and
keep later outcomes out of inputs. relflow does not enforce these application
rules. Fit application preprocessing state on training data and reuse it for
validation and prediction.

Attach an ordered [preprocessor](preprocessing.qmd) with
`preprocessor=prepare` or `preprocessor=(clean, enrich)`. Processing happens
before sampling, shuffling, and model batching. The source and processed Arrow
schemas must remain stable within each split across partitions and epochs.

For prediction, `retain=("payment_id",)` keeps a processed identifier in the
output for downstream joins. See [Batch inference](batch-inference.qmd).

## Polars

For applications that already use in-memory eager frames, `PolarsDataModule`
converts each frame to Arrow once and uses the same pipeline. Collect a
`LazyFrame` explicitly before passing it in.

## Files and restartable sources

Each split also accepts a `pa.RecordBatch`, Arrow Dataset, file path or glob,
`rf.source(...)`, or a callable returning a fresh reader or iterable of Arrow
batches. A reader itself is one-shot; wrap its creation in a callable when
repeated epochs need it.

Use `rf.source(...)` to configure a directory or glob explicitly:

```python
data = rf.ArrowDataModule(
    train=rf.source("payments/history/train", format="parquet"),
    validate=rf.source("payments/history/validation/*.parquet", format="parquet"),
)
```

`rf.source(...)` adds explicit format, schema, filesystem, and partitioning
configuration when needed. Keep nested structs and lists in their Arrow form.
Use an explicit schema when values are empty, entirely null, or ambiguous.
Local `file://` URIs preserve Windows drive letters and URI-encoded path
characters; ordinary local file paths remain supported.

## DuckDB

Install `relflow[duckdb]` to use SQL queries as named splits. `DuckDBDataModule`
opens an existing database file read-only and streams query results as Arrow
batches through the same preprocessing and batching pipeline.

Suppose your application maintains `warehouse/payments.duckdb` with a
`payment_observations` table. Each row has the payment fields above, a unique
`payment_id`, and a `dataset_split` column assigned by the application:

```python
observations = """
    SELECT payment_id, trxns
    FROM payment_observations
    WHERE dataset_split = $split
    ORDER BY payment_id
"""

data = rf.DuckDBDataModule(
    database="warehouse/payments.duckdb",
    train=observations,
    validate=observations,
    parameters={
        "train": {"split": "train"},
        "validate": {"split": "validate"},
    },
)
```

Each split accepts one `SELECT` statement, including a query beginning with
`WITH`. Bind values through `parameters`, keyed by split: a mapping supplies
named parameters such as `$split`; a sequence supplies positional `?`
parameters. Parameters are bound by DuckDB rather than interpolated into SQL.

Omitting `database` creates a fresh in-memory database for each scan. This is
useful for queries that read files directly:

```python
data = rf.DuckDBDataModule(
    predict="""
        SELECT payment_id, trxns
        FROM read_parquet('warehouse/scoring/*.parquet')
        ORDER BY payment_id
    """,
)
```

The module stores the database path, SQL, parameters, and connection settings.
Each scan opens its own connection and Arrow reader in the consuming process,
then closes both. Pass a database path or `":memory:"`; live connections,
relations, and tables registered on another connection are not inputs. Nested
lists and structs remain Arrow-backed, and an empty result retains its schema.
Close writable connections to a database file before starting read-only scans.

Workers and distributed ranks replay the full query. Distributed ranks then
take disjoint model batches, and local data workers alternate the Arrow
batches the query yields before preprocessing, so each worker prepares only
its share. Prediction, an `epoch_size` cap, and dataset-scoped preprocessors
keep every worker on the complete stream, taking turns on finished batches.
Use a deterministic `ORDER BY` with a unique key and keep query results stable
for the duration of each pass across workers and ranks. Data may change
between passes if its Arrow schema stays stable. The module does not
materialize a shared snapshot, and adding workers repeats database work.

`ingress_rows` defaults to `4096` and controls the Arrow batch size requested
from DuckDB; `model.batch_size` controls the final model batches. Each connection
defaults to one DuckDB thread. Override connection settings with `config`, such
as `config={"threads": 2}`. The usual `ArrowDataModule` options, including
sampling, shuffling, retention, and workers, also apply. Partition-scoped
[preprocessors](preprocessing.qmd) run on streamed Arrow batches converted to
eager Polars frames; dataset-scoped preprocessing is unsupported for these
restartable query sources.

## File scan resources

File sources freeze the selected file paths, schema, sizes, and modification
times, then create a fresh filesystem and dataset for each scan. Exhausting or
closing the scan releases its readers and clients; the source and data module
retain only the description and manifest between passes. Storage failures keep
their original cause and include the discovery or scan stage in the traceback.
The data pipeline also closes suspended scans when preprocessing fails or an
`epoch_size` limit ends the iteration.

This matters for native S3: Arrow's process-wide shutdown callback can block
while native clients remain alive, as described in an
[upstream report](https://github.com/apache/arrow/issues/50188). RelFlow releases
its scan resources before interpreter shutdown and continues to use native
PyArrow S3 without another transport dependency. Application-owned datasets,
filesystems, and unfinished iterators have their own lifetimes; close active
iterators when stopping a scan early. The change does not establish that every
native Arrow shutdown hang has the same cause or replace runtime supervision.

[Preprocessing](preprocessing.qmd) attaches to any of these sources. If a
split fails to bind, see [Troubleshooting](../reference/troubleshooting.qmd).
